content: 1. Ceftazidime, Ceftibuten, Cefuroxime, Cephalexin, Ciprofloxacin, Clarithromycin, Clindamycin, Demeclocycline, Doxycycline, Erythromycin (various forms), Gemifloxacin, Levofloxacin, Metronidazole, Minocycline, Nitrofurantoin, Ofloxacin, Paromomycin, Penicillin VK: These antibiotics may reduce the effectiveness of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. 2. Cenobamate: This drug decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Women using oral contraceptives with cenobamate should be advised to use additional or alternative non-hormonal birth control methods. 3. Ceritinib, Cimetidine, Cyclosporine, Dasatinib, Elvitegravir/Cobicistat/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir DF, Fedratinib, Finererone, Flibanserin, Fluconazole, Fluvoxamine, Itraconazole, Ketoconazole, Lenacapavir, Levoketoconazole, Lomitapide, Nicardipine, Nilotinib, Posaconazole, Quinupristin/Dalfopristin, Ribociclib, Rucaparib: These drugs increase the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting hepatic or intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended, and dose adjustments may be necessary for some drugs. 4. Clobazam: This drug may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives by weakly inducing CYP3A4 enzymes. Additional non-hormonal contraception is recommended. 5. Ethinylestradiol and Benzodiazepines (e.g., Clonazepam, Diazepam, Midazolam): Ethinylestradiol may inhibit the clearance of benzodiazepines that undergo oxidation, leading to increased serum concentrations. Caution and monitoring are advised. 6. Dabrafenib, Darunavir, Elagolix, Lorlatinib, Lumefantrine, Mitotane, Rufinamide: These drugs decrease the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing hepatic or intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended in some cases. 7. Danicopan: This drug increases plasma concentrations of BCRP substrates, including ethinylestradiol. Dose adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 8. Ethinylestradiol and Antidiabetics (e.g., Exenatide, Insulin Aspart, Insulin Degludec, Insulin Detemir, Insulin Glargine, Insulin Glulisine, Insulin Lispro, Insulin NPH, Insulin Regular Human, Liraglutide, Metformin): Ethinylestradiol may impair glucose tolerance, reducing the hypoglycemic effects of antidiabetic medications. Glycemic control should be monitored in diabetic patients. 9. Ethinylestradiol and Growth Hormone Analogs (e.g., Lonapegsomatropin): Oral estrogens may reduce serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) response to growth hormone analogs, potentially requiring higher growth hormone doses. 10. Ethinylestradiol and Selegiline: Oral contraceptives inhibit the N-demethylation of selegiline, increasing its levels. Caution and monitoring are advised. 11. Ethinylestradiol and GLP-1 Agonists (e.g., Lixisenatide): GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying, which may affect the absorption of oral medications, including contraceptives. Oral contraceptives should be taken at least 1 hour before or 11 hours after lixisenatide administration. 12. Ethinylestradiol and Mifepristone: Mifepristone reduces the effects of ethinylestradiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Backup contraception is recommended. 13. Ethinylestradiol and Momelotinib: Momelotinib, a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the toxicity of ethinylestradiol by plasma protein binding competition. Dose adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 14. Ethinylestradiol and Nemolizumab: Nemolizumab may decrease ethinylestradiol levels by increasing CYP enzyme activity. Monitoring and dosage adjustments may be required. 15. Ethinylestradiol and Otesaconazole: Otesaconazole, a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the effects and toxicity of BCRP substrates, including ethinylestradiol. Dose adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 16. Ethinylestradiol and Siltuximab: Siltuximab may downregulate CYP450 activity in the liver due to infection or inflammation, potentially altering ethinylestradiol metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 17. Ethinylestradiol and Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir: These drugs may decrease ethinylestradiol levels by increasing its metabolism, possibly through CYP2C9 or CYP1A2 induction. Additional non-hormonal contraception is recommended for the remainder of the cycle. 18. Ethinylestradiol and Ropinirole: Ethinylestradiol increases ropinirole levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 19. Ethinylestradiol and Lamotrigine: Combination oral contraceptives significantly decrease lamotrigine plasma concentrations, likely due to induction of lamotrigine glucuronidation. Monitoring and dose adjustments may be necessary. 20. Ethinylestradiol and Mexiletine: Ethinylestradiol increases mexiletine levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 21. Ethinylestradiol and Ramelteon: Ethinylestradiol increases ramelteon levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 22. Ethinylestradiol and Rasagiline: Ethinylestradiol increases rasagiline levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 23. Ethinylestradiol and Lapatinib: Ethinylestradiol increases lapatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 24. Ethinylestradiol and Lomitapide: Ethinylestradiol increases lomitapide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Lomitapide doses should not exceed 30 mg/day. 25. Ethinylestradiol and Grapefruit: Grapefruit increases ethinylestradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 26. Ethinylestradiol and Green Tea: Ethinylestradiol increases green tea levels by decreasing its elimination. Caution and monitoring are advised. 27. Ethinylestradiol and Hemin: Ethinylestradiol decreases the effects of hemin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Larger doses of hemin may be required. 28. Ethinylestradiol and Hyaluronidase: Estrogens in large systemic doses may render tissues partially resistant to hyaluronidase, requiring larger amounts for equivalent dispersing effects. 29. Ethinylestradiol and Olanzapine: Ethinylestradiol increases olanzapine levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 30. Ethinylestradiol and Liraglutide: Ethinylestradiol may impair glucose tolerance, reducing the hypoglycemic effects of liraglutide. Glycemic control should be monitored in diabetic patients. 31. Ethinylestradiol and Moxifloxacin: Moxifloxacin may reduce the effectiveness of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. Caution and monitoring are advised. 32. Ethinylestradiol and Nafcillin: Nafcillin decreases ethinylestradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 33. Ethinylestradiol and Istadefylline: Istadefylline increases ethinylestradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose adjustments of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates may be necessary. 34. Ethinylestradiol and Lemborexant: Ethinylestradiol increases lemborexant levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Lower nightly doses of lemborexant are recommended. 35. Ethinylestradiol and Fostemsavir: Fostemsavir inhibits BCRP transporters, potentially increasing the effects and toxicity of BCRP substrates. Avoid coadministration or adjust the dose of BCRP substrates. 36. Ethinylestradiol and Momelotinib: Momelotinib, a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the toxicity of ethinylestradiol. Dose adjustments of BCRP substrates may be necessary. 37. Ethinylestradiol and Lomitapide: Ethinylestradiol increases lomitapide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Lomitapide doses should not exceed 30 mg/day. 38. Ethinylestradiol and Rucaparib: Rucaparib increases ethinylestradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose adjustments of CYP3A4 substrates may be necessary. 39. Ethinylestradiol and Siltuximab: Siltuximab may downregulate CYP450 activity in the liver due to infection or inflammation, potentially altering ethinylestradiol metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 40. Ethinylestradiol and Lomitapide: Ethinylestradiol increases lomitapide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Lomitapide doses should not exceed 30 mg/day. 41. Ethinylestradiol and Rucaparib: Rucaparib increases ethinylestradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose adjustments of CYP3A4 substrates may be necessary. 42. Caution and monitoring are advised.
